MUMBAI: Children below 12 years will not be allowed to use lifts or escalators without adult supervision. Any violation will invite revocation of the lift licence of the building complex or establishment.The state govt has notified the Maharashtra Lifts, Escalator and Moving Walks Rules, 2026, introducing stricter safety, maintenance and licensing requirements for lifts, escalators and moving walks. The rules also prohibit the employment of persons below 18 years as lift operators. They place greater responsibility on building owners and equipment owners for maintenance and safety, making it mandatory for approved contractors to inspect and maintain lifts, escalators and moving walks at least once a month. In addition, the equipment must undergo an annual audit and testing by the licensee or an authorised contractor, with the report submitted to the electrical inspector.The new rules prescribe additional safety features for lifts, including CCTV, an automatic rescue device (ARD) and an overload protection device (OLPD). Existing lifts without these systems must be fitted with them within one year of the rules' notification.The framework also makes accident reporting time-bound. Every accident must be reported to the electrical inspector and the local police station within 24 hours.The rules specify how disused lifts, escalators and moving walks must be secured. Owners must either remove the equipment or ensure it is in a safe mechanical condition after disconnecting from power. All gates, door openings and access points must be securely locked or barricaded to prevent unauthorised entry into lift wells and escalator or moving-walk installations.Disused escalators and moving walks cannot be used as stairs or walkways.To improve emergency response, lift maintenance contractors must provide a 24x7 call-attendance service at their service stations to promptly respond to complaints and emergency calls.The rules also tighten licensing conditions. No licence to operate a lift, escalator or moving walk will be granted unless the installation complies with the applicable National Building Code or Bureau of Indian Standards codes of practice, as well as the Unified Development Control and Promotion Regulations and their provisions governing such installations. They also restrict modifications that could compromise safety. Licensees cannot make additions or alterations that change the basic characteristics of the equipment or affect the safe operation of the installation and the safety of users, maintenance personnel or others in its vicinity.
Article Summary: Children under 12 years of age must be accompanied by an adult while using lifts and escalators. Maharashtra Lifts, Escalator and Moving Walks Rules, 2026, introduced stricter safety, maintenance and licensing requirements. All lifts must be fitted with additional safety features within one year of the new rules.

Article Title: Your salary may be rising, but how much more can you actually afford? Inflation explained in 10 charts
Article Text:
What's getting costlier and why, explained in 10 charts

Inflation is back above 6%: What's driving the bills

Food inflation and CPI continues to rise

What's driving up inflation

The price pinch: Who expect it the most

Kitchenomics: Why your grocery bill keeps climbing

What got cheaper and costlier in your kitchen

Then vs Now: Same Rs 1,000, smaller grocery haul

What Rs 1,000 get you

Rural India or urban India: Who is feeling the bigger pinch?

Are salaries keeping up with rising prices?

Is your salary hike enough to beat inflation

Where does your paycheque go

Breather or burden: Will prices finally cool down?

Relief on two fronts

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Imagine this: It's the first of the month and you have just received that much-awaited notification: “XYZ salary credited to your bank account”.The sky turns pink, well, for a moment.Enter the monthly budget busters: rent, groceries, phone recharge, utility bills, EMIs, skincare haul and that long-pending friends' group outing. Before the week ends, you're already waiting for your next paycheque!But if your shopping list hasn't changed since last month, why are you paying more for it? The answer is rising prices, and consumers expect the ‘mehengai ki maar’ to continue.According to the RBI's September 2026 Inflation Expectations Survey, households expect inflation to reach 10% over the next 12 months, up from 9.4% in July.Back in October, India's retail inflation was already higher than the RBI's upper limit of 6%, touching 6.09%. Food inflation was even higher, standing at 8.94%.And that's where the pinch is felt most. You can put off buying a new phone or skip a weekend outing, but milk, vegetables, pulses and cooking oil are hard to do without. As their prices rise, you end up spending more on the same shopping list, leaving less money for other expenses.Inflation was relatively low in the early months of 2026, but things began changing from May as the economic fallout of the West Asia conflict started reflecting more prominently in everyday expenses. Rising global crude oil prices led to multiple hikes in petrol and diesel prices in May, pushing up transportation and production costs.Meanwhile, adverse weather conditions and seasonal supply pressures drove up food prices. Retail inflation rose from 3.48% in April to 3.93% in May and continued climbing over the following months, crossing 5% in September and breaching the RBI's upper tolerance limit of 6% in October.A closer look at household expenses shows where some of the pinch is coming from.Beyond the kitchen, eating out and accommodation costs have risen by 10.06%, while personal care and miscellaneous goods and services have become 10.14% costlier.Transport costs are up 5.84%, with higher fuel prices adding to the cost of travelling and moving goods. So, whether it is your grocery run, dinner out or daily commute, several everyday expenses are taking a bigger bite out of your wallet.So, what's behind the rising price tags?There isn't just one culprit. Weather disruptions can affect crop supplies, while global tensions, trade restrictions and supply-chain problems can make commodities more expensive. Add higher fuel and fertiliser costs to the mix, and producing and transporting everyday goods becomes costlier too.Paramdeep Singh, founder of Long Tail Ventures, told TOI that food prices are increasingly shaped by domestic supply conditions and global developments. “Weather disruptions, volatile energy and fertiliser costs, trade restrictions and supply-chain inefficiencies all contribute to price pressures,” he said.When monthly expenses rise faster than your income, there is less money left to put away. In simple terms, inflation chips away at your purchasing power, the same salary buys fewer things than it did earlier. And even when inflation cools, it does not mean prices fall. It simply means they are rising at a slower pace.For example, consider a household earning Rs 60,000 a month and spending Rs 50,000. If monthly expenses rise by 6% to Rs 53,000, savings drop from Rs 10,000 to Rs 7,000. That's a 30% dent in savings, even though expenses have risen by just 6%.Singh says, “The bigger concern is the cumulative erosion of purchasing power. Even when inflation moderates, prices don't necessarily fall.” That's why household savings often tell a more complete story than inflation figures alone.Food is one of the biggest reasons household budgets are feeling the pinch. It made up 34.78% of the new Consumer Price Index (CPI) basket in October, with food inflation at 8.94%. Even home-cooked meals aren't escaping inflation, with veg thalis up 12% and non-veg thalis up 9%.Some kitchen staples have seen particularly sharp price jumps. Onion prices surged 116.22% year-on-year, while garlic became 60.74% costlier. Ginger and lemons also saw steep increases of 48.32% and 47.30%, respectively. In the illustrative Gurugram grocery basket, sugar prices rose 21.4% and milk prices increased 7.1% over the year. Edible oil, too, became 7.1% costlier.Shunil Tripathi, SEBI SMART trainer and an NCFE-empanelled resource person, says the biggest concern is that these are everyday purchases that households cannot avoid. “A family may delay buying a phone, but it cannot delay buying dal, oil or milk,” he says.He attributes the rise largely to supply-side pressures, particularly the conflict in West Asia and higher petroleum prices. Since fuel is used across industries, any increase in its cost can push up transportation expenses and, in turn, the prices of everyday goods — from vegetables to packaged food.Tripathi shared an example of a grocery basket based on local market prices in Gurugram. Last year, a household could buy the listed items for Rs 1,000. This year, the same basket costs Rs 1,050, even though the family has reduced its biscuit purchase from two packets to one.Had the family bought the same quantities as last year, the bill would have been around Rs 1,071, a 7.1% increase. So, it is paying more but taking home less.The inflation burden is not evenly distributed across the country. Rural households are facing higher price pressures than their urban counterparts.MoSPI data show that rural inflation climbed to 6.63% in October, compared with 5.41% in urban areas. Food inflation was also higher in rural India at 9.09%, against 8.68% in urban India.The difference matters because food purchases form a regular and unavoidable part of household spending. Higher prices can therefore put pressure on rural budgets even when the overall national inflation number appears relatively moderate.There are also considerable differences across states. Among states, Tamil Nadu recorded the highest combined retail inflation at 7.29% in October. Telangana followed at 7.26%, Andhra Pradesh at 7.25%, Madhya Pradesh at 7.19% and Odisha at 7.17%.Puducherry, a Union Territory, recorded an even higher rate of 7.96%. At the other end, Delhi's combined inflation stood at 3.80%.These differences show why the experience of inflation can vary depending on where a household lives. The national figure is an average, but the actual price pressure depends on the items people buy and the local markets they depend on.As everyday expenses continue to rise, a salary hike can feel like a welcome relief, offering some cushion against bigger bills. But once the monthly expenses are paid, the extra money may not leave as much in your pocket as you had expected.According to Aon's salary increase survey, India Inc was expected to offer average salary hikes of 9.1% in 2026, compared with 8.9% in 2025. On paper, that may look like a decent cushion against rising prices. But does it really stretch far enough?For starters, these are only averages, and not everyone gets the same pay rise. The real impact also depends on where a household spends most of its money. Grant Thornton Bharat's India's Financial Resilience Report 2026 found that 62% of respondents believe their income growth will not be enough to keep pace with future inflation. Among those aged 25-34, the share was even higher at 70%.Tripathi says incomes have broadly held up over the past year, although the picture varies across employees. Government employees received dearness allowance revisions linked to inflation, while private-sector salary hikes depended on performance and individual outcomes. However, when household budgets get tighter, families often cut back on discretionary spending to protect essentials. As he puts it, “Essentials were protected, and 'wants' were cut. ”So, will a salary hike really make you richer? Not necessarily. What matters is how much you can retain after meeting your monthly expenses. For instance, even a 5% reduction in a household's monthly budget of Rs 50,000 can free up Rs 2,500 a month, or Rs 30,000 annually.Adhil Shetty, CEO of BankBazaar, says households should focus on protecting their cash flow without compromising long-term financial security. “When prices rise faster than income, the first thing that tends to help is building a buffer, roughly a few months of expenses kept aside for emergencies,” he said.He also recommends maintaining an emergency fund covering 3-6 months of essential expenses, prioritising repayment of high-interest debt and reviewing regular spending to identify costs that may have quietly crept up.Ultimately, it is not just about how much extra money lands in your payslip, but how much is left after groceries, bills and other everyday needs. The biggest risk is quietly sacrificing tomorrow's savings to maintain yesterday's lifestyle.Will your grocery bills finally give you some breathing room, or is more price trouble waiting around the corner? The answer will depend on food supplies, farm output and global commodity prices over the next few months.Fresh winter crop arrivals could help bring down prices of some food items. However, global fuel prices and transportation costs could continue to keep everyday goods expensive.Shetty says stable global commodity prices and better agricultural output could help inflation cool gradually. Tripathi, meanwhile, believes the current price pressure is largely supply-driven. He points out that raising interest rates cannot directly bring down crude oil prices or freight charges.“Higher interest rates can cool demand, but they cannot lower the cost of crude oil or reduce freight charges,” Tripathi says. In his view, cheaper fuel and smoother supplies are key to easing the pressure.Bringing down the cost of everyday essentials and leaving households with more money to spend will both be important.In the short term, better food supplies, improved stock management and targeted support for vulnerable households can help ease the burden. Over the longer term, investments in cold storage, farm-to-market transport and agricultural productivity can help prevent sudden price spikes.Singh says relief needs to address both essential costs and household incomes. “Targeted food supply interventions, better inventory management and focused support for vulnerable households can ease pressure,” he says.While targeted support can reach households within weeks, these structural improvements will take longer to deliver results.Ultimately, real relief from inflation is not just about a lower number on paper. It means being able to buy everyday essentials, pay the bills and still have enough left to save, without constantly having to reshuffle the monthly budget.
Article Summary: Inflation was relatively low in the early months of 2026, but things began changing from May. Rising global crude oil prices led to multiple hikes in petrol and diesel prices in May. Weather disruptions, volatile energy and fertiliser costs, trade restrictions and supply-chain inefficiencies all contribute to price pressures.

Article Title: Nvidia Q3 results: Revenue jumps 103% to $115.8 billion; announces $0.25 per-share dividend
Article Text:
Nvidia delivers blockbuster Q3

Nvidia Q3 results

Jensen Huang admits mistakes, signals willingness to return

Board refuses to bring back Huang

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nvidia Q3 results: Nvidia investors finally have something to cheer about as the chipmaker reported a blockbuster third quarter, with revenue soaring more than 100% year-on-year.The company reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter ended October 25, 2026, marking a 103% increase from the year-ago period and a 20% rise from the previous quarter. Its GAAP earnings per diluted share stood at $2.70, while non-GAAP earnings per diluted share came in at $2.68.The timing of the results is particularly significant as the tech giant is caught up in a series of controversies surrounding its former boss, Jensen Huang, alleged to have had a relationship with a Chinese ‘spy’, apart from two other women.Also Read| As Nvidia founder Jensen Hunag says, he is ready to come back as CEO; Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress says board has determined it will not reinstate Huang and that is Board's The company reported GAAP gross margins of 74.8% and non-GAAP gross margins of 74.9% for the quarter. Nvidia also returned $28.1 billion to shareholders during the third quarter of fiscal 2027 through share buybacks and cash dividends.Back in September 2026, Nvidia's Board of Directors approved an additional $150 billion in share repurchase authorisation, with no expiration date. At the end of the third quarter, approximately $227.3 billion remained available under the programme.Nvidia's next quarterly cash dividend will be $0.25 per share, payable on December 23, 2026, to shareholders on record as of December 2, 2026.Commenting on the quarterly performance, Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer of Nvidia, highlighted the company's continued momentum and technology leadership.“Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” Kress said in a press statement.She also expressed confidence in the company's technology roadmap, adding, “Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater."While Nvidia's financial performance remained in focus, former CEO Jensen Huang made his first public comments since being caught up in the alleged Chinese Spy Scandal.In a statement on X, Huang thanked those who had supported him and his family over the past week. He also spoke about his journey to the United States and described becoming an American citizen as one of the proudest moments of his life."Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life."Huang described Nvidia as his life's work and said building the company alongside his colleagues had been a privilege. He also acknowledged that his personal conduct had fallen short of the standards expected at the company and said he regretted the difficulties caused to its board."Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honour. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation," he added.His statement also signalled his willingness to return as the company's chief executive if the board backed his reinstatement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he said.However, any possibility of Huang returning to the leadership role was ruled out by Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones. Speaking at the beginning of the company's quarterly earnings call on Tuesday, Jones said the board had unanimously accepted Huang's resignation and had no intention of bringing him back as CEO."The board of directors unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said.The chairman's remarks came just hours after Huang indicated that he would be open to returning to the company if invited.The controversy centres on Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese Spy. The former CEO resigned last week following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a Chinese woman who worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company.The allegations have also brought scrutiny to relationships linked to Huang both within and outside Nvidia. His latest statement acknowledged personal mistakes and expressed his commitment to cooperating with the board's independent investigation.
Article Summary: N Nvidia reports blockbuster third quarter, with revenue soaring more than 100% year-on-year. Company reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter ended October 25, 2026, marking a 103% increase from the year-ago period. Former CEO Jensen Huang made his first public comments since being caught up in the alleged Chinese Spy Scandal. Huang acknowledged that his personal conduct had fallen short of the standards expected at the company and said he regretted the difficulties caused to its board.

Article Title: Most Delhi buildings that fell in recent times weren’t found ‘dangerous’
Article Text:
A local clearing the debris manually

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines





NEW DELHI: The building collapse in east Delhi has once again exposed gaps in MCD ’s mechanism to identify and act against dangerous structures, particularly in unauthorised colonies.Despite surveying more than 30 lakh houses ahead of the monsoon this year, the civic body had declared only 51 buildings ‘dangerous’, while several structures that subsequently collapsed were not flagged as unsafe.Regarding Tuesday’s incident, MCD officials said the building near a railway track in Jwala Nagar was constructed on encroached railway land more than 40 years ago. The 20 sq yard structure, comprising ground, first and second floors, was built using T-iron beams and stone slabs.“The building was old and situated close to the railway line. It emerged during local inquiries that vibrations caused by the movement of trains may also have contributed to the incident” said an MCD official.MCD standing committee chairperson Satya Sharma has directed officials to conduct regular inspections of dangerous and dilapidated buildings, and take timely action if they identify risks.According to officials, no visible signs of damage were found during monsoon inspections that could have helped identify the structure as dangerous.They also pointed to protection available to unauthorised constructions existing before 2014.However, another official clarified, “Protection under Special Provision Act does not extend to buildings violating safety standards or encroaching upon govt land. In this case, both conditions were violated as the structure was within the railway corridor.”Under DMC Act, MCD can take demolition action, except in areas falling under the jurisdiction of the cantonment, NDMC or DDA. Under Section 348, a building can be declared dangerous, followed by a notice under Section 349 directing occupants to vacate it.However, buildings in Jwala Nagar, Satya Niketan, Hauz Rani and Said-ul-Ajaib were not declared dangerous before collapsing, raising questions over the effectiveness of the exercise. Officials said inspections are based largely on visual assessments and residents’ complaints.Following a meeting held with the Union home secretary, MCD earlier this month submitted a draft roadmap to Delhi govt for a structural audit of buildings. It flagged the need for additional manpower, structural experts and funds. However, no progress has been made so far.Delhi has an estimated 32.5 lakh buildings, while Census 2027’s first phase recorded nearly 76 lakh houses.“Considering nearly 70% of Delhi’s built-up area comprises unauthorised zones, govt should consider setting up a council of structural engineers where residents can seek safety audits if they find buildings tilted or damaged, even if authorised,” the official said.Meanwhile, Delhi BJP spokesperson Praveen Shankar Kapoor wrote to the mayor and municipal commissioner, demanding MCD re-establish its wing to check dangerous buildings and conduct a comprehensive 30-day survey. He claimed seven dilapidated buildings had collapsed in recent months, including in Jwala Nagar and Chawri Bazar, and an under-construction hotel in Paharganj.
Article Summary: The building collapse in east Delhi has exposed gaps in MCD ’s mechanism to identify and act against dangerous structures. Despite surveying more than 30 lakh houses ahead of the monsoon this year, the civic body had declared only 51 buildings ‘dangerous’ Several structures that subsequently collapsed were not flagged as unsafe.

Article Title: Govt reviews Adani project; company says cost remains 5,675 crore
Article Text:
The Maharashtra forest minister Ganesh Naik reviewed Adani Green Energy's hydroelectric project amid ongoing controversies

MUMBAI: State forest minister Ganesh Naik chaired a meeting on Tuesday to review Adani Green Energy Ltd's (AGEL) proposed 1,500 MW pumped storage hydroelectric project at Tarali in Patan taluka of Satara district, which ran into a controversy following the company's projection of a lower environmental cost on the adjoining region which is ecologically sensitive.According to official sources, the govt may consider withdrawing the forest department's demand seeking 4% of the total project cost towards wildlife conservation around the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve and Koyna Wildlife Sanctuary.The 4% demand was made on AGEL by way of a letter issued by Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (Wildlife).The company has clarified that the total estimated capital cost of the project is Rs 5,675 crore, while the Rs 56.75 crore cited earlier as project cost referred only to the phase dealing with survey, investigation, geological exploration, engineering studies, detailed design, field investigations, testing and other preliminary activities for feasibility assessment. It said wildlife clearance was sought for these preliminary works. The proposal was cleared by the State Board for Wildlife in March, and 1% of the applicable cost related to the survey and investigation proposal was deposited with the govt.Tuesday's meeting, attended by AGEL officials, reviewed project requirements, environmental conservation measures and recommendations from the forest department, with focus on balancing infrastructure development and ecosystem protection.Officials also discussed the eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) around the wildlife sanctuary. With no specific ESZ notification in place, a 10-km radius applies on the project as per Supreme Court guidelines.In a written clarification to the chief wildlife warden and the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (Wildlife), AGEL said the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) granted environmental clearance in Feb last year and the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board granted "consent to establish" in April. The company stated no forest land is involved, and a non-forest land NOC has already been obtained.After completing formalities and obtaining a go-ahead from the State Board for Wildlife for site investigations, the company said it submitted a fresh proposal on Nov 5 seeking National Board for Wildlife approval for the full project, with the project cost stated as Rs 5,675 crore, matching the cost mentioned in the environmental clearance.The state forest department issued a stop-work notice on Nov 13 directing work at the project site to be halted, citing commencement of work without National Board for Wildlife approval.AGEL's clarification comes after Satara's Honorary Wildlife Warden, Rohan Bhate, last month flagged an alleged discrepancy in the project cost declared to the state govt, stating it was shown as ₹56.75 crore instead of ₹5,675 crore.In representations to the NBWL, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), and the chief minister, he sought an independent inquiry, arguing that an understated cost could amount to misrepresentation and could affect wildlife conservation contributions linked to project value.
Article Summary: The Maharashtra forest minister Ganesh Naik reviewed Adani Green Energy's hydroelectric project amid ongoing controversies. The company has clarified that the total estimated capital cost of the project is Rs 5,675 crore. The state forest department issued a stop-work notice on Nov 13 directing work at the project site to be halted.

Article Title: Water crisis: El Nino may hit Hyderabad hardest among all major metros
Article Text:
As El Nino conditions continue, Hyderabad is bracing for a severe drinking water crisis.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines





HYDERABAD: Come December, Hyderabad could find itself at the epicentre of a drinking water crisis, with El Nino conditions threatening to push its key reservoirs, Singur and Manjeera, close to running dry. The city's daily water deficit could exceed 1,000 MLD, up from the existing shortfall of nearly 600 MLD, making Hyderabad one of the worst-hit metros in the country.The two reservoirs together supply 480 MGD of water, accounting for nearly 20% of Hyderabad's total supply of 2,600 MLD. The city's estimated daily demand, however, stands at 3,200 MLD.In comparison, Bengaluru is estimated to face daily deficits of 500 to 600 MLD amid the El Nino effect, while Mumbai's shortfall is pegged at around 500 MLD, according to various reports. Delhi, like Hyderabad, is staring at a deficit of 1,000 MLD. However, the capital has recorded 14% excess rainfall this season, offering some cushion against the looming crisis.Besides, Delhi's water deficit is a long-standing problem, prompting authorities to put multiple contingency measures in place to manage peak demand. According to the Delhi Jal Board, these include emergency supply networks, wastewater recycling and groundwater extraction through tube wells across the city, particularly along the Yamuna and Ganga.Hyderabad, meanwhile, is facing a different challenge. The city's CURE area - including Rangareddy, Medchal-Malkajgiri and Hyderabad - has received around 240 mm less rainfall than usual this year, translating into a 33% deficit.The already wide demand-supply gap has also widened suddenly, catching authorities off guard.Adding to the concerns, experts say that rainfall in the catchment areas of Hyderabad's reservoirs has been considerably lower than in those supplying Mumbai and Delhi this season."That makes Hyderabad more vulnerable, particularly as summer approaches and groundwater extraction becomes increasingly difficult," said an official from the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI). He added: "The situation could become particularly critical from Feb onwards, when groundwater availability is expected to dip sharply."The city's reservoirs are already under considerable stress, with storage levels at Singur at 7%, Manjeera at 17%, Osmansagar at 54% and Nagarjunasagar at 57%. Mumbai, in contrast, is in a relatively comfortable position. The city has seven major drinking water sources, including Bhatsa and Modak Sagar. Official records show that they together hold over 80% of their storage capacity, following rainfall of around 2,500 mm this monsoon, against the normal 2,490 mm.Experts say that healthy storage levels should help the Maharasthra capital tide over the summer, despite the El Nino effect, and sustain supplies for the next seven to eight months.Bengaluru, too, has a relatively better reservoir buffer. The Krishna Raja Sagara Dam in Mandya district and other reservoirs in the Cauvery basin together have around 50% of their storage capacity, according to available estimates. Also, each of the reservoirs can service any part of the city, unlike Hyderabad."While Hyderabad faces the prospect of 3.5 lakh consumers in its IT corridor, who are entirely dependent on Manjeera, being left with dry taps as early as next month, Bengaluru might still see some supply reaching its most critically affected pockets, such as Bommanahalli and Chickpet. This is because the city has several other pumping stations drawing water from the Cauvery and supplying different parts of the city," said a water management expert from Bengaluru. Experts fear Hyderabad's situation could persist right up to April."The period between Dec and April is expected to see very little rainfall. Given that Hyderabad, which normally receives 800-900 mm of annual rainfall, has received nearly 40% less this year, the dry spell could further affect its drinking water availability," said a professor at the IISc.Water board officials say they have rolled out emergency measures to tackle the crisis while drawing up longer-term plans to address the shortfall. An additional 40 MGD (180 MLD) is proposed to be sourced from the Godavari to compensate for the shortage, while another 45 MLD will be made available by adjusting supplies from the Krishna source.
Article Summary: El Nino conditions threaten to push key reservoirs, Singur and Manjeera, close to running dry. Hyderabad's daily water deficit could exceed 1,000 MLD, making it one of the worst-hit metros in the country. Bengaluru is estimated to face daily deficits of 500 to 600 MLD amid the El Nino effect. Mumbai's shortfall is pegged at around 500 MLD.
